title: Traffic engineering and safety
summary: The traffic sign shapes and colours are the most reliable marks — triangle with red border is cautionary, circular is mandatory, rectangular is informatory, with STOP an octagon and GIVE WAY an inverted triangle. For flow theory, q equals k times v is the fundamental relation, and the crucial insight is that flow is MAXIMUM at the optimum density, so adding vehicles beyond that point reduces flow. Safety questions turn on the collision diagram, which converts an accident record into a specific engineering remedy.

sections.heading: Traffic flow theory
sections.body:
**The three fundamental parameters:**

| Parameter | Symbol | Units | Definition |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Flow (volume)** | **q** | vehicles/hour (or PCU/hour) | Vehicles passing a point per unit time |
| **Density (concentration)** | **k** | vehicles/km | Vehicles occupying a unit length at an instant |
| **Speed** | **v** | km/h | **SPACE MEAN speed** |

**The fundamental relation:**

> **q = k × v**

**The speed must be the SPACE MEAN speed**, not the time mean speed. Using the time mean speed overstates the flow, because the time mean is always the larger — it weights fast vehicles equally with slow ones, whereas at any instant more slow vehicles are present in a given length.

**Greenshields' linear model** is the simplest and most examined relationship:

> **v = v_f (1 − k/k_j)**

where **v_f** is the **free-flow speed** and **k_j** the **jam density**. Substituting into q = kv:

> **q = v_f (k − k²/k_j)**

which is a **parabola** in k. Differentiating and setting to zero:

> **Maximum flow occurs at k_optimum = k_j / 2** and **v_optimum = v_f / 2**
> **q_max = v_f k_j / 4**

**So the capacity occurs at HALF the jam density and HALF the free-flow speed** — three results worth memorising as a set.

**The consequence is the most useful insight in traffic theory:**

> **Beyond the optimum density, ADDING more vehicles REDUCES the flow.**

That is the onset of congestion, and it explains the everyday experience of a motorway that carries fewer vehicles per hour when it is jammed than when it is busy but flowing. The **q–k curve** rises to a peak at k_opt and then falls back to zero at the jam density — where there are many vehicles but none moving, so the flow is zero.

**It also explains why ramp metering and traffic management work**: by restricting entry to keep the density **below** the optimum, the flow through the section is **increased**, even though fewer vehicles are admitted at any moment. Counter-intuitive, and a direct consequence of the parabola.

**The two branches of the q–k curve:**

| Branch | Condition | Character |
|---|---|---|
| **k < k_opt** | **Free flow / stable** | Higher speed, lower density; a **disturbance dies out** |
| **k > k_opt** | **Congested / forced flow, unstable** | Lower speed, higher density; a **disturbance propagates backward as a shock wave** |

**Related quantities:**

| Quantity | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Headway (time)** | Time between successive vehicles passing a point; **q = 3600/h_t** |
| **Spacing (distance headway)** | Distance between successive vehicles; **k = 1000/h_s** |
| **Time occupancy** | Proportion of time a detector is occupied |

**Capacity:**

| Term | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **Basic capacity** | Under **ideal** conditions — the theoretical maximum |
| **Possible capacity** | Under **prevailing** conditions |
| **Practical (design) capacity** | With a margin, giving an acceptable **level of service** |

> **Theoretical single-lane capacity ≈ 1000 V / S**, with S the average spacing in metres

**Levels of service (LOS)**, A to F:

| LOS | Condition |
|---|---|
| **A** | **Free flow**; drivers unaffected by others |
| B | Reasonably free flow |
| **C** | **Stable flow**, but manoeuvring restricted — a common design target |
| D | Approaching unstable flow |
| E | **At capacity**; unstable |
| **F** | **Forced or breakdown flow**; stop-and-go |

Rural highways are designed to **LOS B or C**, urban roads to **C or D** — the difference reflecting that urban land is too expensive to provide free flow, and that urban drivers accept more congestion.

**Design service volumes (IRC 106)** for urban roads: about **1800 PCU/hour** per lane for a divided carriageway at LOS C, less for undivided and for roads with frequent access.

sections.heading: Traffic control devices
sections.body:
**Four categories:**

| Device | Assigns / conveys |
|---|---|
| **Traffic signs** | **Regulation, warning or information** |
| **Road markings** | **Channelisation and delineation** |
| **Traffic signals** | Right of way in **TIME** |
| **Islands and channelisation** | Right of way in **SPACE** |

**The signals-in-time and islands-in-space distinction** is a neat way to hold the difference, and it is examinable.

**Requirements of any traffic control device** — four, and each is a genuine design criterion:

| Requirement | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **Command ATTENTION** | Adequate size, contrast, illumination, position |
| **Convey a CLEAR, SIMPLE meaning** | Standard shapes and symbols; no ambiguity |
| **Allow adequate TIME to respond** | Placed well in advance of the hazard |
| **Command RESPECT** | Reasonable and enforceable |

**The fourth deserves emphasis** because it is the one most often violated: a device that is **ignored** actively **undermines the whole system**. A speed limit set unrealistically low, a signal that stays red with no conflicting traffic, or a no-entry that everyone disregards teaches drivers that signs need not be obeyed — and that habit transfers to the signs that matter. Setting realistic, enforceable controls is therefore a safety measure, not a concession.

**Traffic signs — the classification by SHAPE and COLOUR**, which is the most reliable source of marks in the subchapter:

| Class | Shape | Colour | Message | Legal force |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **CAUTIONARY (warning)** | **Equilateral TRIANGLE, apex up** | **RED border**, white ground, black symbol | **Warns of a hazard ahead** — bend, gradient, school, narrow bridge | **None** — the driver must exercise judgement |
| **MANDATORY (regulatory)** | **CIRCULAR** | Red border (prohibitory), or **blue** (positive instruction) | **Must be obeyed** — speed limit, no entry, one way, compulsory direction | **Enforceable — disobedience is an offence** |
| **INFORMATORY** | **RECTANGULAR** | Blue or green ground | **Guides** — direction, distance, place names, facilities | None |

**Two signs deliberately break their own shape rule**, because they are the most critical and must be **unmistakable even if partly obscured or seen from behind**:

| Sign | Shape |
|---|---|
| **STOP** | **OCTAGON** |
| **GIVE WAY** | **INVERTED TRIANGLE** |

**The legal distinction between mandatory and cautionary** is the substance of the classification: a **mandatory** sign is **enforceable**, and disobeying it is an offence; a **cautionary** sign carries **no penalty** for proceeding — it warns, and the driver must then judge. That is precisely why they use **different shapes** rather than merely different symbols, so the *kind* of message is recognised before the symbol is read.

**Retro-reflective sheeting** is required for night visibility. A sign that cannot be read after dark is **worse than none**, because it gives the appearance of a signed road without the substance — and much of the traffic on Nepal's highways moves at night.

**Road markings:**

| Marking | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **Centre line — broken** | Lane separation; **overtaking permitted** |
| **Centre line — CONTINUOUS** | **NO overtaking / no crossing** |
| Double continuous | No crossing in either direction |
| Continuous with broken alongside | Crossing permitted from the broken side only |
| **Edge line** | Delineates the carriageway edge; valuable at night and in rain |
| **Stop line** | Where vehicles must stop |
| **Zebra crossing** | Pedestrian priority |
| Lane lines, turn arrows, chevrons, hatching | Channelisation |
| **Rumble strips** | Audible and tactile warning |

**Materials**: **thermoplastic (hot applied)** — the standard, durable and retro-reflective with glass beads; **road paint** — cheaper, shorter life; **preformed tape**; **raised pavement markers (cat's eyes)** — valuable in fog and rain.

**Traffic signals** assign right of way in time.

**Terminology:**

| Term | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **Cycle** | One complete sequence of all phases |
| **Phase** | The part of the cycle allocated to one movement or set of movements |
| **Interval** | A period during which the indications do not change |
| **Green time** | The green period for a phase |
| **Lost time** | Time not usefully used — start-up delay plus clearance |
| **Saturation flow** | The maximum flow that can discharge during a continuous green |

**Webster's method** for the optimum cycle:

> **C₀ = (1.5 L + 5) / (1 − ΣY)**

where **L** is the total lost time per cycle and **ΣY** the sum of the critical flow ratios (**y = q/s**, actual flow ÷ saturation flow).

**Green time is then allocated in proportion to the critical flow ratios y_i.**

**The crucial observation about ΣY:**

> As **ΣY approaches 1**, the cycle length **tends to infinity** — the intersection is at **capacity** and **NO cycle length will work**.

That is a genuinely useful result: it tells the engineer that a signal timing problem has become a **geometry or demand problem**. The remedies are then to **add capacity** (widen the approach, add a turning lane, use a flyover) or **reduce demand** (divert traffic, restrict turns), not to keep adjusting the timings. Practical cycle lengths are **40 to 120 seconds** — below 40 too much time is lost in changes, above 120 the delay to waiting traffic becomes unacceptable.

**Signal warrants** — when a signal is justified: **traffic volume** on both approaches, **pedestrian volume**, **accident experience**, and the need for **coordination**. Installing a signal where volumes do not warrant it **increases delay and accidents**, because drivers disregard a signal that seems unnecessary.

**Coordination** of signals along an arterial (a **green wave**) is achieved by offsetting the start of green by the travel time between intersections. It works well in one direction and is a compromise in two.

**Intersections and their treatment:**

| Type | Character |
|---|---|
| **Uncontrolled** | Priority by rule only; suitable at very low volumes |
| **Priority (STOP or GIVE WAY)** controlled | The minor road yields |
| **Channelised** | Islands guide the movements, reducing the conflict area |
| **Rotary (roundabout)** | Converts **crossing** conflicts into **merging and diverging** |
| **Signalised** | Right of way separated in time |
| **Grade separated (flyover, underpass, interchange)** | Conflicts eliminated entirely |

**The rotary's principle** is worth understanding: it **converts crossing conflicts into merging and diverging conflicts**, which are far less severe because the relative speed and the collision angle are both much lower. It suits **moderate flows from 3 to 7 approaches**; at high volumes it **locks up** (because entering traffic cannot find gaps) and a signalised or grade-separated solution becomes necessary.

**Rotary design parameters (IRC 65)**: **weaving angle about 15°**, adequate **weaving length**, **entry deflection** to slow traffic, and a central island large enough to prevent traffic crossing straight through.

sections.heading: Road safety
sections.body:
**Causes of accidents** — the conventional four groups:

| Group | Examples |
|---|---|
| **Road user** | Speeding, drunk driving, fatigue, inattention, inexperience, wrong overtaking, disobeying signs — **the largest single group** |
| **Vehicle** | Brake or steering failure, tyre burst, defective lights, **overloading** |
| **Road and its environment** | Inadequate **sight distance**, poor **geometry**, defective surface, poor **drainage**, lack of markings or signs, obstructions, **no guard rail** |
| **Traffic and other** | Mixed traffic, pedestrian conflict, animals, weather, poor visibility |

**The engineer's responsibility lies in the third group**, and it is larger than it appears: many accidents attributed to "driver error" occur at a location where the geometry **invited** the error — a bend sharper than its approach suggests, a sight distance inadequate for the prevailing speed, an unmarked hazard. That is why **accident locations cluster**, and why treating the location works even though the immediate cause was a driver.

**Accident study — the two diagrams, and their combination is the substance:**

| Diagram | Shows |
|---|---|
| **COLLISION diagram** | Each accident drawn **in its actual position**, with **ARROWS showing the direction and movement** of each vehicle, plus symbols for type, severity, date, time and weather |
| **CONDITION diagram** | A **scaled plan of the physical features** — road width, surface, obstructions, sight lines, signs, markings, drainage, abutting development |

**The collision diagram is DIAGNOSTIC, not statistical**, and that is its value: because the accidents are drawn in their actual positions and movements, a **PATTERN becomes visible** that a table of numbers conceals.

**Patterns and the remedy each suggests:**

| Pattern | Likely cause | Remedy |
|---|---|---|
| Many **rear-end** collisions | Sudden stopping; inadequate sight distance | Improve **SSD**, advance warning, signal timing |
| Many **right-angle** collisions | Right of way not clear | **STOP / GIVE WAY**, or signals |
| Many **right-turn** collisions | Conflicting turning movements | **Channelisation**, a dedicated turning phase |
| Many **head-on** collisions | Overtaking on a two-way road | Median, no-overtaking marking, widening |
| Concentration **at night** | Poor visibility | **Lighting**, retro-reflective signs and markings |
| Concentration **in the wet** | Loss of friction | **Skid resistance**, drainage, camber correction |
| **Pedestrian** collisions | No safe crossing provision | Zebra crossing, refuge, footpath, signal phase |
| **Single-vehicle run-off** | Geometry, or a fixed object | Superelevation check, guard rail, remove the object |

**That table is the whole point of the exercise**: it converts an accident record into a **specific engineering intervention** rather than a general call for care. A question asking what a collision diagram is used for is asking for exactly this.

**Accident statistics and rates.** Numbers alone cannot be compared between locations of different exposure, so they are **normalised**:

| Rate | Basis |
|---|---|
| **Accident rate per 100 million vehicle-kilometres** | For a **length** of road |
| **Accident rate per million entering vehicles** | For an **intersection** |
| Accidents per 1000 population, or per 1000 vehicles | For a region — a policy measure |
| **Severity index** | Fatal and serious accidents as a proportion |

**Black spots** are locations with an accident frequency or rate **significantly above the network average**. The systematic approach:

> **Identify black spots (from records) → DIAGNOSE (collision and condition diagrams) → TREAT → evaluate BEFORE-and-AFTER**

**The before-and-after evaluation is the step most often omitted**, and it is what makes the process a discipline rather than a guess: without it, there is no evidence that the treatment worked, and no learning for the next location. The evaluation must allow for **regression to the mean** — a site identified because of an unusually bad year would have improved somewhat anyway — which is why a control group or a longer period is used.

**Road safety audit** is the preventive counterpart: a **formal, independent examination** of a road scheme at the **design stage** (and at completion, and after opening) to identify safety hazards **before** they cause accidents. Its value is that it costs almost nothing to move a sign, widen a shoulder or improve a sight line **on a drawing**, and a great deal to do so after construction.

**Engineering safety measures**, by category:

| Category | Measures |
|---|---|
| **Geometry** | Adequate **sight distance**, correct **superelevation and radius**, flatter gradients, **set-back clearance** at curves |
| **Cross-section** | Adequate width, **shoulders**, **median**, **footpath**, safe roadside |
| **Surface** | **Skid resistance**, evenness, drainage, no standing water |
| **Roadside** | **Guard rails and parapets**, removal or protection of **fixed objects**, breakaway posts, clear zone |
| **Control devices** | Signs, markings, signals, delineators, studs |
| **Lighting** | At junctions, curves, pedestrian crossings, built-up areas |
| **Traffic calming** | Speed humps, rumble strips, raised crossings, chicanes, **narrowing** |
| **Pedestrian and cyclist provision** | Footpaths, crossings, refuges, segregated tracks |

**The "clear zone" concept** deserves note: a vehicle leaving the carriageway should have a **traversable area free of hazards** in which to recover. Trees, poles, culvert headwalls and unyielding signposts within that zone convert a run-off into a fatal collision. The remedies are to **remove**, **relocate**, **make breakaway**, or **shield** them — in that order of preference.

**The Nepali context** for road safety, which questions increasingly reflect:

| Factor | Character |
|---|---|
| **Hill roads with steep drops** | A run-off accident is frequently **fatal**; **parapets and guard rails** are therefore critical, and their absence is a widespread deficiency |
| **Mixed traffic** | Pedestrians, animals, tractors, motorcycles and heavy buses sharing a narrow carriageway |
| **Overloaded buses and trucks** | Overloading affects braking, stability and the pavement alike |
| **Inadequate sight distance** on narrow hill roads | Blind bends, no set-back clearance |
| **Poor maintenance** of markings, signs and drainage | The controls that exist cease to function |
| Night travel on unlit highways | — |
| **Landslide and rockfall** hazard | A safety issue as much as a maintenance one |

**Bus accidents on hill roads are Nepal's characteristic road safety problem**, and the contributing factors are engineering as much as behavioural: **inadequate carriageway width and radius for the vehicles using the road**, **missing parapets** at exposed locations, **poor surface and drainage**, and **overloading** that raises the centre of gravity and lengthens the braking distance. Each is addressable, and the addressable ones are the engineer's responsibility.

formulas.label: Fundamental relation of traffic flow
formulas.expression: q = k × v     (v must be the SPACE MEAN speed)
formulas.note: Using time mean speed overstates the flow, since it is always the larger of the two.

formulas.label: Greenshields' model and capacity
formulas.expression: v = v_f(1 − k/k_j) ;   q_max = v_f k_j/4 at k_opt = k_j/2 and v_opt = v_f/2
formulas.note: Beyond the optimum density, ADDING vehicles REDUCES flow — the onset of congestion.

formulas.label: Headway and spacing relations
formulas.note: Links the macroscopic parameters to individual vehicle behaviour.

formulas.label: Theoretical lane capacity
formulas.expression: C ≈ 1000 V / S     (S = average spacing in metres)
formulas.note: Design service volume about 1800 PCU/hour per lane at LOS C for a divided urban carriageway.

formulas.label: Traffic sign classification
formulas.expression: CAUTIONARY = triangle, red border. MANDATORY = circular. INFORMATORY = rectangular. STOP = octagon. GIVE WAY = inverted triangle.
formulas.note: Mandatory signs are legally enforceable; cautionary signs warn only. Hence different SHAPES, not just symbols.

formulas.label: Webster's optimum cycle length
formulas.note: As ΣY → 1 the cycle tends to infinity — the intersection is at capacity and NO timing will work.

formulas.label: Accident rates
formulas.expression: per 100 million vehicle-km for a LENGTH ;   per million entering vehicles for an INTERSECTION
formulas.note: Raw numbers cannot be compared between locations of different exposure.

formulas.label: Black spot treatment sequence
formulas.expression: Identify → DIAGNOSE (collision + condition diagram) → treat → evaluate BEFORE-and-AFTER
formulas.note: The evaluation is the step most often omitted, and must allow for regression to the mean.
